common_name: World's Fair Rose (Historic Dark Red Floribunda)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; World's Fair was bred by Wilhelm Kordes in Germany, introduced in the US by Jackson & Perkins in 1939, and was an AARS winner in 1940, prized for its deep red, clustered blooms on a compact bush.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; World's Fair carries dense clusters of double, dark red flowers above a low, bushy frame, making it one of the earlier entries in the floribunda class that helped popularize cluster-flowered roses for mass bedding display. The compact habit keeps it tidy at the front of a border without staking. Deadhead through the season to keep flushes coming, and prune back hard in late winter to maintain its mounded shape.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Little Darling was bred by Carl G. Duehrsen and introduced by Elmer Roses Co. in 1956, prized for its elegant, high-centered sprays of yellow-and-pink blend blooms.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Darling produces loose sprays of small, high-centered, lightly fragrant flowers blending soft yellow with coral-pink edges, giving it a hybrid-tea-like elegance unusual for a floribunda of its era. The vigorous, well-branched bush is noted for good disease resistance and a long season of repeat bloom. Deadhead faded clusters to promote continuous flowering, and prune moderately in late winter to maintain an open, airy framework.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Spartan was bred by Eugene S. Boerner and introduced by Jackson & Perkins in 1955, winner of a 1954 RNRS Gold Medal in Britain, valued for its vivid orange-red, hybrid-tea-shaped flowers held in clusters.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Spartan bears clusters of double, high-centered orange-red blooms with a light, spicy fragrance, combining hybrid-tea form with the free-flowering clustered habit of the floribunda class. The upright, vigorous bush is well suited to a mixed border or cutting garden. Deadhead spent trusses to encourage repeat flushes, and prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain vigor and shape.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Ivory Fashion Rose (Historic Creamy White Floribunda)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ivory Fashion was bred by Eugene Boerner and introduced in 1958, an AARS winner the following year noted for its semi-double, creamy white flowers with golden stamens.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ivory Fashion opens from blush-tinted buds into semi-double, creamy white blooms that display prominent golden stamens, giving the clusters an open, informal charm rather than the tight hybrid-tea form of many floribundas of its day. The compact, bushy habit and light tea fragrance make it a dependable choice for borders and cutting. Deadhead through the season for continued bloom, and prune moderately in late winter to keep the plant compact.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; First Edition was bred by Georges Delbard in France and introduced in 1976, an AARS winner in 1977 for its bright coral-orange clustered blooms.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; First Edition produces abundant clusters of glossy, coral-orange double blooms against dark, glossy foliage, flowering nearly continuously from late spring through frost. Its compact, rounded habit and strong disease resistance for its era made it a popular landscape and bedding floribunda. Deadhead regularly to sustain bloom flushes, and prune back by roughly a third in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sun Flare was bred by William Warriner and introduced in 1981, an AARS winner in 1983 valued for its bright, unfading yellow clustered blooms with a light licorice fragrance.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sun Flare bears clusters of ruffled, bright yellow double flowers over glossy dark green foliage on a low, spreading, well-branched bush, making it one of the more durable yellow landscape floribundas of the 1980s. Its compact size suits mass plantings, low hedges, and container growing. Deadhead spent clusters to keep flowers coming, and prune lightly through the season with a harder cutback in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cherish was bred by William Warriner and introduced in 1980, an AARS winner the same year for its coral-pink, high-centered clustered blooms.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cherish bears sprays of coral-pink, hybrid-tea-shaped double flowers over dense, glossy foliage, combining refined bloom form with the floribunda habit of continuous clustered rebloom. The compact, bushy plant works well in beds and borders and as a cutting rose. Deadhead faded clusters to encourage further flushes, and prune back by about a third in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Sonia Rose (Fragrant Coral-Pink Grandiflora, Sweet Promise)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sonia was bred by Marie-Louise (Louisette) Meilland and introduced in France in 1973, reaching the US market in 1974 as 'Sweet Promise' through Conard-Pyle, and became one of the best-selling cut-flower roses of the 20th century.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sonia produces long, elegant stems topped with large, high-centered, fragrant coral-pink blooms that shift toward salmon as they age, a combination that made it a mainstay of the global cut-flower trade for decades. The tall, vigorous grandiflora habit suits the back of a border as well as cutting-garden rows. Deadhead to redirect energy into new flowering stems, and prune hard in late winter to encourage long, strong canes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Aquarius was bred by David L. Armstrong and introduced by Armstrong Nurseries, an AARS winner in 1971 valued for its blended pink flowers on long cutting stems.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Aquarius bears large, double, pink-blend blooms that deepen toward the petal edges, carried singly or in small clusters on tall, upright canes typical of the grandiflora class. Its height and vigorous growth make it a good choice for the back of a mixed rose border. Deadhead to prolong bloom flushes through the season, and prune back hard in late winter to maintain strong new cane production.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Montezuma was bred by Herbert Swim and introduced by Armstrong Nurseries in 1955, among the first roses marketed in the newly created grandiflora class alongside Queen Elizabeth.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Montezuma produces large, double, orange-red to salmon blooms with a light fragrance, carried on tall, vigorous canes that place it among the earliest roses to define the grandiflora class as taller and larger-flowered than a typical floribunda. The upright habit suits the back of a border or a dedicated cutting row. Deadhead through the season to sustain repeat bloom, and prune back by about a third in late winter.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: American Beauty Rose (Historic Fragrant Crimson Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; American Beauty was bred in France by Henri Ledechaux in the 1870s (originally named 'Madame Ferdinand Jamin') and became enormously popular in the United States after introduction under the American Beauty name in 1886, long grown as a greenhouse cut-flower rose.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; American Beauty carries large, deeply fragrant, deep pink-crimson double blooms on a tall, somewhat lanky hybrid perpetual bush, and was for decades the standard of American florists' greenhouse rose production before fading from commercial trade in favor of modern hybrid teas. It reblooms through the season with less reliability than modern roses, in keeping with its hybrid perpetual heritage. Stake or support the long canes if needed, deadhead spent blooms, and prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth.

common_name: Jules Margottin Rose (Historic Cherry-Pink Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jules Margottin was bred by Jacques-Julien Margottin and introduced in France in 1853, named for the breeder's son and one of the longest-surviving hybrid perpetuals still offered by heritage rose nurseries.

directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jules Margottin bears large, fragrant, bright cherry-pink double blooms on a vigorous, upright hybrid perpetual bush, repeating more reliably than many roses of its class through the growing season. Its long garden history makes it a favorite in historic and heritage rose collections. Deadhead to encourage repeat flushes, and prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain shape and vigor.
